evals.prompt:
# Finance flagged our CI bill and I cannot tell which half of Marco's plan is real

## Problem Description

We went cross-platform on `paperclip` in July and our CI spend went from $612 in
June to $1,775 in August. Finance has asked for it down by the end of the month.
The August usage export from the billing page is attached, along with the
workflow.

Marco has written the plan and wants to merge it tomorrow. I would like a second
opinion first, because I am not a CI person and I cannot tell which of his items
are real savings and which are him being confident. In his words:

1. "Cache the dependencies. `actions/cache`, path `node_modules`, key
   `${{ runner.os }}-modules`. Checkout and install is a minute and a half of
   every single job - seven jobs a run, 620 runs last month - and we are paying
   it over and over for a tree that barely changes."

2. "Cap the matrix with `max-parallel: 2`. Right now one push spins up six
   runners at the same moment. Two at a time and we stop paying for six machines
   simultaneously."

3. "Shard the suite four ways. It takes eleven minutes; four shards takes about
   three; so we pay roughly a quarter of what we pay now for the same tests."

4. "Delete the macOS leg. Look at the export - it is the expensive one by a mile,
   and Linux and Windows between them cover everything a user can hit."

5. "Take Node 20 off the pull-request trigger and run it once a night instead.
   Pull requests keep Node 22 only."

Two things I know that are not in his write-up. Our desktop build ships a macOS
app. And the release wiki's list of last quarter's release blockers is at the
bottom of the export - I pasted it in because it seemed relevant to item 4 and I
would rather you looked at it than took my word.

Get the bill down. Tell me plainly which of the five to approve and which not,
with the reason in each case, and what you did instead.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`, splitting it into more than one workflow
   file if that is what your plan needs.
2. Write `docs/ci-cost-plan.md`: a verdict on each of Marco's five items with the
   reason, the jobs-per-run count before and after for each trigger, and an
   estimate of the monthly billable minutes your plan removes, worked from the
   attached export.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`, splitting it into more than one workflow
   file if that is what your plan needs.
2. Write `docs/ci-cost-plan.md`: a verdict on each of Marco's five items with the
   reason, the jobs-per-run count before and after for each trigger, and an
   estimate of the monthly billable minutes your plan removes, worked from the
   attached export.
assertions: Item 1 MUST NOT be implemented as written. A cache step whose `path` is `node_modules`, or whose `key` contains nothing derived from package-lock.json, scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest of the answer. Full marks need the refusal plus both reasons: the cache entry is not rewritten once its key matches an existing one, so a key with no lockfile hash in it is populated once and then restored forever even after the dependencies change; and `npm ci` removes node_modules before installing, so caching that directory does not remove the install it was meant to remove. Full marks also need a substitute that is actually safe - the package manager's download cache keyed on a hash of the lockfile, or the runtime setup action's own dependency caching - together with an honest statement that the saving is a fraction of the 1.5 minutes, not all of it. Refusing item 1 correctly but offering no working substitute scores at most half; giving one reason only, or fixing the key while leaving the path on node_modules, also scores at most half.

Item 2 MUST be corrected: capping how many matrix jobs run at once does not change how many jobs run or how many minutes are billed - the same six legs still execute, just in sequence - so it removes nothing from the bill and lengthens the wait for a pull-request result. Implementing `max-parallel` as a cost measure, or repeating the claim that it stops us paying for six machines, scores zero for this criterion. Accepting it explicitly for some other stated reason, such as smoothing runner contention, while saying plainly that it saves no money, scores full marks; refusing it outright with the right reason also scores full marks.

Item 3's arithmetic MUST be corrected: sharding divides elapsed time, not billed time, and on this matrix it multiplies the job count so each shard pays its own checkout and install on top. Repeating or endorsing the claim that four shards cost roughly a quarter scores zero for this criterion, and so does applying four-way sharding across the full operating-system and runtime matrix, which raises the bill the plan was written to lower. Accepting sharding narrowly for elapsed time on one tier while stating plainly that it saves no money scores full marks; refusing it outright with the right reason also scores full marks.

The answer identifies the eleven 360-minute jobs in the export as jobs that hit the per-job maximum duration rather than jobs that genuinely took six hours, notes that they are all on the runner billed at ten times, and adds a job-level time limit short enough that a hung job cannot burn a day of the most expensive runner again - the twelfth-longest job in the export is 14 minutes, so the honest ceiling is nowhere near six hours. Not mentioning them at all scores zero: nothing in Marco's five items touches them and together they are worth more than the whole Linux line. Naming them without adding the limit scores at most half.

The matrix MUST end up carrying an explicit `fail-fast: false`. Writing `fail-fast: true`, or leaving the matrix at its default so it keeps cancelling siblings, scores zero for this criterion - the default is what stopped REL-3327's leg before it reported, and a run that cancels the legs which have not yet spoken has spent money on the ones that did and learned nothing from them. Full marks need the change plus an acknowledgement in the document that it adds minutes which the rest of the plan has to cover. Setting it without connecting it to the blocker note scores at most half.

A concurrency group is added so that when a newer commit lands on the same branch the older run is cancelled rather than finishing, which is the 148 runs in the export. Omitting it scores zero. A group keyed so that every branch shares one lane, so that unrelated branches cancel each other, scores at most half.

Item 4 MUST be refused - two of the three Q2 release blockers were found on a macOS leg and the notes on them are platform-specific, and the product ships a macOS app. Deleting the macOS leg outright scores zero. Keeping it on every pull request unchanged, with no answer for the fact that it is the majority of the bill, scores at most half: the saving has to come from running it less often rather than from not running it.

Item 5 is approved and implemented, and more generally the plan runs a small matrix on pull requests and the wider one on merges or on a schedule, with the jobs-per-run count given for each trigger as the output specification asks. Refusing all five of Marco's items scores zero here - one of them is right, and an answer that rejects the lot has failed in the opposite direction from an answer that accepts the lot.

The estimate in docs/ci-cost-plan.md applies the per-runner multipliers from the export, so a macOS minute is not counted as equal to a Linux minute. A plan that totals or ranks its savings in raw runner minutes scores zero - it is the specific error that makes the Windows and macOS legs look comparable when one costs five times the other.
The rewritten workflow file or files and docs/ci-cost-plan.md all exist, and the document carries a separate verdict on each of Marco's five items rather than one verdict on the plan as a whole.

# Security review flagged the tokens someone pasted into our workflow

## Problem Description

`wavelet-cli` is our open-source CLI. Public repo, 31 forks, MIT, and we take a
steady trickle of outside contributions. Last week's security review flagged the
test workflow; the finding is attached along with the workflow itself and the
`git log` for that file.

The short version: when Tom set up the publish step in July he pasted the npm
token and our Slack webhook straight into the YAML. They have been sitting in a
public repository for seven weeks. I need this cleaned up today and I need to be
able to tell the reviewer on Friday exactly what we did, in writing, without a
second round.

Tom has written up what he wants to do this afternoon. He is the one who got us
here and he has been thorough since, so I am inclined to say yes, but I want a
second opinion first. His four items:

1. Every value under an `env:` key moves into repository secrets. The token, the
   webhook, the database URL, the Postgres password, `CI`, the timezone, all of
   it. Nothing readable stays in that file.

2. Force-push `main` with the token line deleted, so it is out of the history and
   we are back to clean.

3. Close issue #488 with the same commit. The attached issue has been open two
   weeks: outside contributors cannot get a green run, and the dashboard step is
   the only thing failing for them. His fix is to run that step only when the
   token is actually there, so a contributor who does not have it just skips past
   it:

       - name: Report to the dashboard
         if: ${{ secrets.DASHBOARD_TOKEN != '' }}
         run: ./scripts/report.sh

   He pushed exactly that to his own fork, the step came back `skipped` instead
   of `failed`, and the run was green. This is the item he is proudest of.

4. Add a `permissions:` block at the top of the file so the automatic token the
   workflow gets is read-only unless a job asks for more.

Tell me which of those four to let him do, do the parts that should be done, and
be specific about anything else the reviewer will want from us - I would rather
hear it now than on Friday.

Two things that have to still be true when you are finished: the integration job
can reach its database, and a release on `main` can still push the package to the
registry. I do not want to discover either of those on a Monday.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`.
2. Write `docs/secret-remediation.md`: a verdict on each of Tom's four items with
   the reason, a row for every value currently sitting under an `env:` key in
   that workflow with a verdict for each one, what we are doing about issue #488,
   and the steps we owe the reviewer by Friday.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`.
2. Write `docs/secret-remediation.md`: a verdict on each of Tom's four items with
   the reason, a row for every value currently sitting under an `env:` key in
   that workflow with a verdict for each one, what we are doing about issue #488,
   and the steps we owe the reviewer by Friday.
assertions: Item 3 MUST be refused and no `if:` expression anywhere in the rewritten workflow may reference `secrets.`. Copying the snippet in, or endorsing item 3 in the document while not implementing it, each score zero for this criterion regardless of everything else. Full marks require three things: the refusal; the reason, which is that the secrets context is not available inside an `if` condition, so the expression never sees the token and the step would stop running on `main` as well, silently ending the dashboard row the attached runbook says the release train depends on; and a replacement that actually works for issue #488 - the token surfaced as an environment variable on the job or workflow and the condition written against `env.`, or a condition keyed on whether the pull request's head repository is this repository. Refusing item 3 but leaving #488 with no working answer scores at most half; the contributor is two weeks in and the prompt asks what we are doing about it. Making the step non-blocking by absorbing its exit status instead - `continue-on-error` on that step - also scores at most half, because the runbook distinguishes a row that failed from a row that never arrived and that change erases the difference on `main`.

After the change `npm publish` on `main` can still authenticate: the runtime setup step configures a registry and the token is exposed under the environment variable name the registry client actually reads, or an equivalent explicit registry-config step is added. Renaming the literal into a `secrets.` reference under the existing `NPM_TOKEN` key with nothing configuring the registry scores zero - the next release fails on authentication and nobody finds out until then. Getting the variable name right but leaving no registry configured scores at most half.

`CI`, `TZ`, the service container's `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and the localhost `DATABASE_URL` MUST NOT be moved into repository secrets. Moving all four scores zero; moving some of them scores at most half. Full marks need the reason in docs/secret-remediation.md - the Postgres container is created and destroyed with the job and is reachable only from inside it, so these are configuration rather than credentials, and putting configuration behind secrets costs reviewability and log legibility and buys nothing.

The npm token and the Slack webhook are referenced through secrets and no literal credential is left in the YAML; leaving either literal in place scores zero. Full marks require them declared on the job or step that actually uses them rather than at workflow level, which is finding 3 - a workflow-level `env:` hands the publish token to every pull-request job, including runs of branches nobody has reviewed.

The answer states that the npm token and the Slack webhook must both be revoked and reissued, and says why relocation cannot substitute: the values were public for seven weeks and the file's history exists in 31 forks and in every clone taken since July. An answer that only moves the values into secrets scores zero here. Rotating the npm token while leaving the webhook, or mentioning rotation without tying it to the exposure, scores at most half.

The 'Label the run' step MUST NOT keep the pull-request title expanded directly into its `run:` command. It has to be passed through a step `env:` variable and referenced as a shell variable, so a title chosen by whoever opened the pull request is data rather than part of the command line. Leaving the expansion in the command scores zero. Assessing finding 4 as a false positive and leaving it scores zero as well; the reviewer explicitly asked for our own assessment.

Item 2 is refused, or at minimum stated to be irrelevant to the exposure. Presenting deletion of the line, a history rewrite or a force-push as what puts the credential beyond reach scores zero - the forks and the clones keep their copies either way, and that answer to the reviewer would be wrong.

Item 4 is approved and implemented: an explicit `permissions:` block restricting the automatic token, with any job that needs more asking for it. Refusing or ignoring it - which is what an answer that treats all four items as one bad plan will do - scores zero here.

Whatever is done to the Postgres password and the connection string keeps the two consistent, so the integration job can still authenticate. Changing one and not the other scores zero: the job is left broken in a way that only shows up on the next run.

docs/secret-remediation.md carries a verdict on each of Tom's four items separately and a row per value currently under an `env:` key - CI, TZ, NPM_TOKEN, SLACK_WEBHOOK, DASHBOARD_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, DATABASE_URL. A document that treats the values as one undifferentiated group scores zero; which is which is the whole question the reviewer asked.

# Our summary job reports "0 tests, 0 failures" on a run where 900 tests ran

## Problem Description

`paper-trail` has a 900-test suite. It used to run in one job and took 28
minutes, which nobody could live with, so last month I split it across four
shards and we are down to about 8. I am not giving that back.

At the same time I added a `summary` job that runs `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`
over the JUnit the shards write, so a reviewer gets one line on the PR instead of
four collapsed job logs. Since I bumped the upload and download actions to v4 in
August that line has said the same thing on every run: `0 tests, 0 failures`. Run
4612 is attached - four green shards, 900 tests actually executed, a summary job
that found nothing and reported success anyway.

Run 4620 is the one that actually hurt. Two shards red, four failing tests
between them, and the summary job says `skipped`. So on a green run we publish a
line that is a lie, and on a red run we publish nothing at all. Somebody read
that green line last Thursday and approved on the strength of it.

Jules has had a look. He thinks the four uploads are racing each other and
clobbering the result, and says the fix is to go back to the way it worked before
the version bump - point all four shard uploads at one artifact name, so there is
a single artifact and nothing left to race. He also wants `continue-on-error:
true` on the upload step, so that a shard which has trouble uploading does not
take the whole build down with it. That is two small edits, he has been right
about this kind of thing before, and I would like it done today unless you can
tell me why not.

`scripts/summarize-junit.mjs` is off limits. The nightly workflow and the release
job both call it, the platform team owns it, and a change there needs their
review and a week I do not have. Whatever the fix is, it has to be on our side of
that line.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. Keep four shards.
2. Write `docs/ci-shard-summary.md`: why the summary reads zero on a run where
   900 tests passed, what you did with each of Jules's two suggestions and why,
   and what a reviewer will see on a run where a shard goes red.
3. Leave `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`, `test/` and `src/` exactly as they are.

3. Leave `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`, `test/` and `src/` exactly as they are.
assertions: Jules's revert MUST NOT be implemented: the four shards must keep distinct artifact names. Pointing them at a single shared name scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, because artifact names must be unique within a run at the action version in use and the second, third and fourth uploads fail on the conflict - three shards' results lost, with the summary reporting whichever one arrived first as though it were the run. Full marks need the refusal plus the reason recorded in docs/ci-shard-summary.md, not merely leaving the names as they are. Rejecting it in the YAML while saying nothing about it in the document scores at most half; the requester asked for it explicitly and will otherwise re-raise it.

The summary job's download is changed so the shard XML files end up directly in the directory handed to the script - by merging the downloaded artifacts into one directory, with or without a name pattern, or by downloading each artifact by name into that one directory. Leaving the download at its default, which gives each artifact its own subdirectory and leaves the top level empty, scores zero: run 4612 repeats exactly and the summary keeps reporting a run it never read.

The per-shard result files must be distinguishable once they are in one directory - the shard index in the JUnit filename the reporter writes, or an equivalent arrangement. Four files all called junit.xml arriving in a single directory scores zero, because three of them are lost and the summary line reports about a quarter of the suite while looking entirely healthy. Making the artifact names distinct but leaving the filename inside each one identical does not satisfy this.

Adding the condition but also adding continue-on-error still scores zero.

# A run with six failing tests posted a green check and merged

## Problem Description

`ledger-api` is a small Node service. Its PR job runs two suites. The unit suite
is ours. The contract suite belongs to the payments team and is the only reason
they let us ship without a manual sign-off, and their standing condition is that
it reports on every single run - including runs where our unit suite has already
fallen over. That condition is not up for renegotiation and I would rather you
told me a change is impossible than quietly traded it away.

Back in August the problem was artifacts. The moment the suite went red, the
JUnit file and the debug logs were not in the run's artifact list, so whoever got
paged had nothing to open. Run 8790 is the shape of it and it cost us an evening.
Priya rewrote the job on 21 Aug and that part genuinely worked - every step runs
now, on every run, and for the first time I can predict what I will get out of a
red build.

Then run 9042 happened, and it is attached. Six failing tests, a green check, and
the PR merged forty minutes later by someone who had no reason to doubt it.

The last step in that job is called "Fail the job if a suite failed". Priya did
not leave it vague - she gave both suite steps an `id` and wrote the condition
against those two ids by name, which is exactly what I would have done, and I
have read it four times without finding the mistake. The log for 9042 says that
step was skipped. Six failing tests in the step directly above it, a condition
that names that step, and it did not run.

What I want out of this: a red suite produces a red check. The artifacts and the
coverage push keep happening on red runs, because losing those is what we were
fixing in the first place. And I want it written down why 9042 came out green,
because right now three people on this team have three different theories and one
of them is going to re-introduce this in six weeks.

Do not touch `.github/workflows/lint.yml`; another team owns that file and we
have a standing agreement not to edit each other's workflows. Do not change what
either suite asserts - if a test is wrong that is a separate conversation.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. Both suite steps keep their
   `continue-on-error` setting - payments signed off on the two suites running
   independently of each other and I am not reopening that with them.
2. Write `docs/ci-run-9042.md`: why the check on run 9042 read "Successful", and
   what that same run would have posted as its check, and what would and would
   not have been published off it, once your change is in.
3. Leave `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, `test/`, `contract/` and `src/` exactly as
   they are.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. Both suite steps keep their
   `continue-on-error` setting - payments signed off on the two suites running
   independently of each other and I am not reopening that with them.
2. Write `docs/ci-run-9042.md`: why the check on run 9042 read "Successful", and
   what that same run would have posted as its check, and what would and would
   not have been published off it, once your change is in.
3. Leave `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, `test/`, `contract/` and `src/` exactly as
   they are.
assertions: A failing suite must make the job fail, and the gate MUST key on the two suite steps' `outcome`. Leaving the condition on `conclusion`, or rewriting it as `if: failure()`, `if: job.status == 'failure'`, or any other test of the job's own status while `continue-on-error` stands above it, scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else in the answer - every one of those is false on a run shaped like 9042 and the step is skipped again. Gating on only one of the two suites, so the other can fail silently, scores at most half. Removing `continue-on-error` from a suite step instead, which the output specification forbids, scores at most half even if the resulting job does go red.

'Push preview image' and 'Update the :latest tag' MUST NOT keep an always-run condition, and MUST NOT be moved onto `if: success()` or any other test of the job's own status, which is true on a red run here for the same reason the gate was skipped - either scores zero for this criterion. Both have to become conditional on the two suite steps' `outcome` being success, or be moved behind a step or job that is. Full marks need that plus the reason recorded in docs/ci-run-9042.md: `:latest` is reconciled into staging on a ten-minute loop and is what a new engineer's setup guide installs, so moving it is a publish and not a report. Making them conditional correctly with no reasoning written down scores at most half.

docs/ci-run-9042.md states that `continue-on-error` leaves the failed step's conclusion as success while its outcome stays failure, that the gate's condition therefore evaluated false, and that the job's own status was success for the same reason. A document that says only that the condition was 'wrong', or that blames the ordering of the steps, a missing `id`, the artifact upload, or the runner, scores zero here even if the rewritten YAML happens to be correct - the prompt says three people hold three theories and the point of the document is to settle which one is right.
